The api tier has no spare instances, so one failure stops both reads and writes. You will need more api instances for peak anyway, which also gives you the redundancy.

Money is not your problem: {{cost:total.inr}} a month against {{cost:total.budget}}, {{cost:total.spare}} spare. items.text: 'An incident link goes round' failed: the promise is at most 2,000 calls a second, yours is 4,530 calls a second.
GET_PASTE took 602.2 ms at the 99th percentile; the promise is 80 ms. Slowest hop: api at 227 % of capacity.

The db is the bottleneck and also the bill: it runs at 153 % of capacity at the peak and takes 74 % of spend at ₹40,000. Since pastes never change and live at most a day, a cache or cdn front can absorb the repeated opens and let the db carry only writes and misses.

The quiet hour passes with 63 % to spare, writes go lb to api to ids to db at {{path:CREATE_PASTE.p99}} p99, reads at {{path:GET_PASTE.p99}}, and the whole thing costs ₹54,000 against ₹1,50,000. The shape is sound and there is budget headroom to add a caching layer.

review.headline: Reads and budget are fine, but acknowledged writes are lost when the database primary fails

items.text: When the db primary fails, writes that had already been acknowledged to the client were lost. The hidden test 'The database primary fails' failed, and this is the only failing test, so durability is your one broken promise. Point CREATE_PASTE at a path that only acknowledges after the write is on a replica, not just on the primary.
items.ask: Which write acknowledgement does your api return after the db primary dies?

items.text: Both paths still touch the db on every request, reads and writes alike. The read path pays lb 2.0 ms → api 20.8 ms → cache 2.0 ms → db 10.2 ms with the db step at {{path:GET_PASTE.p99}} p99, and the write path pays lb 2.0 ms → api 20.8 ms → ids 0.0 ms → db 15.3 ms. With the cache sitting in front, a write that survives on replicas only, or a db that waits for replicas, can stall those reads.
items.ask: How does a replica read interact with your cache on the read path?

items.text: The incident case and the quiet hour both pass with 24 % to spare on their tightest promise. The api is the busiest component at 57 % of capacity, and the cache at 5 %, so you have headroom to absorb an extra hop or a longer wait on the write side.
This design costs ₹1,14,000 a month; the budget is ₹1,50,000 (24 % to spare).

next.text: Make the db acknowledge a write only once it is durable on a replica, then re-run the primary failure test.

items.text: CREATE_PASTE never lands anywhere. Its route stops short of sql, nosql or objectstore, so a created paste is not durably saved and its id is handed out with nothing behind it. Trace that route until it reaches a store that confirms the write before returning the id.

items.text: GET_PASTE also never reaches a place where the data lives. A read that does not touch sql, nosql or objectstore can only serve empty answers, so opens would fail even if writes worked. Point the read path at the same store that holds the pastes.

items.text: api runs at 15 % of what it can take in 'Lunch time', and 75 % at its busiest ('Dinner time').
This design costs ₹1,82,000 a month; the budget is ₹2,25,000 (19 % to spare).

review.headline: Reads and latency look good, but acknowledged writes are lost when a storage node dies.

items.text: Your kv store acknowledges writes without enough copies, so when a storage node dies the message is gone and both reads and sends fail. This breaks the "never lose an acknowledged message" rule. Make kv wait for a quorum of replicas before it acknowledges a send.
items.ask: Which kv setting decides how many copies must answer before a write is acknowledged?

items.text: When the node dies, requests failed rather than being served from a surviving copy. With one copy per message there is nothing to fail over to. Copies with read repair would let chats keep opening and sending continue during the outage.
items.ask: What does your read path do when the replica it lands on is the one that died?

items.text: The happy path is solid. Lunch and dinner both passed, and both request paths sit well inside the p99 promise with a fast median. The extra hop for id generation costs almost nothing.
Stateless app servers survived an app node dying, and at dinner time api and kv were well short of their limits. There is headroom to spend on replication.
This design costs ₹1,82,000 a month; the budget is ₹2,25,000 (19 % to spare).

items.text: The failing case is durability at kv. When a storage node died, acknowledged SEND_MESSAGE writes were lost, so the store broke the promise that an acknowledged message is never lost. The write path acks before the data is safely on other copies.

GET_SCORE took 433.5 ms at the 99th percentile; the promise is 250 ms. Slowest hop: api at 125 % of capacity.
GET_SCORE goes cdn → lb → api → cache → db: p99 52.2 ms, median 3.8 ms, in 'The toss'.
This design costs ₹1,91,000 a month; the budget is ₹2,60,000 (27 % to spare).

The steady state is healthy: the toss test passed with 27 % to spare, and median read latency was {{path:GET_SCORE.p50}}. The write path also stays quick at {{path:UPDATE_SCORE.p50}} median, so updates are not the thing to fix first.

next.text: Add capacity to the api tier so the last over fits, and then shift reads to be served by the cache at the front so the spike never reaches api.

items.text: In the last over the api tier received {{finding:overloaded:GET_SCORE:api.calls}} against a ceiling of {{finding:overloaded:GET_SCORE:api.expected}}, so it ran at {{load:api.peak}} of capacity and the test failed. The same tier is only {{load:api.rho}} loaded at the toss, so the spike shape is the problem, not the steady state.

items.ask: Why are so few reads answered from the cache, and what would make cache hits the normal case?
items.text: Read p99 was {{finding:p99:GET_SCORE:none.actual}} against a promise of {{finding:p99:GET_SCORE:none.expected}}, with api named as the slowest hop. Meanwhile the cache handles only {{load:cache.calls}} and the db is essentially idle at {{load:db.rho}}, so most reads are paying for the api hop instead of being served near the edge.

Every read still walks cdn, lb, api, cache and db, with the api hop alone costing {{path:GET_SCORE.hops}}. That chain is what pushes p99 past the promise under spike. Reads served from a shared cache key at the front of the path, with the db only on a miss or write, would shorten it.

You have room to spend. The design costs {{cost:total.inr}} a month against {{cost:total.budget}}, {{cost:total.spare}} to spare, and the db dominates cost at {{cost:db.share}}. That headroom lets you add capacity where the spike actually lands.

The steady state is healthy: the toss test passed with {{test:t01-toss.spare}} to spare, and median read latency was {{path:GET_SCORE.p50}}. The write path also stays quick at {{path:UPDATE_SCORE.p50}} median, so updates are not the thing to fix first.

review.headline: Fast and cheap, but the read path dies when the cache restarts mid-over because it falls straight through to a single db

items.text: When the cache restarts mid-over, reads fail at the db. Your cache is treated as the only source of live scores, so a cold cache turns into an outage for fans. The db has capacity headroom, so make the durable score readable directly and let the cache rebuild itself from it.
items.ask: What serves a read while the cache is empty, and how long before the score is fresh again?

items.text: The db has no spare, so if it fails both reads and updates stop. It is also on the critical read path, cdn to lb to api to cache to db. Add replicas and point score reads at a replica, with the writer primary, so a failure does not take the service down.
items.ask: Where does a score read go if the primary db is down?

items.text: api runs at 7 % of what it can take in 'The toss', and 71 % at its busiest ('The last over').

The happy path is solid. Median read latency is {{path:GET_SCORE.p50}}, well under the promise, and the toss, last over and server dies tests all passed with room to spare. Keep this shape and fix the cold cache case rather than redesigning.
This design costs ₹1,37,000 a month; the budget is ₹2,60,000 (47 % to spare).

next.text: Redesign the cold cache moment: make the durable score readable straight from the db with a replica behind it, and have the cache refill from that, then rerun the cache restart test.

review.headline: Reads fail when the cache restarts mid-over because they fall through to a database with no spare capacity

items.text: When the cache restarted mid-over, reads fell through to db and failed. Your GET_SCORE path ends cache → db, so a cold or restarting cache pushes the entire read spike onto the database instead of absorbing it.
items.ask: Where should a read get the score while the cache is empty after a restart?

items.text: db is the only durable store and the judge flags it as having no spare. Both the write path and any cache rebuild depend on it, so an outage there stops the score and every read that misses the cache.
items.ask: How would you keep the score durable and still serve reads if db became unavailable?

items.text: api runs at 7 % of what it can take in 'The toss', and 71 % at its busiest ('The last over').
Cost sits well inside the budget at ₹1,37,000 a month, 47 % to spare, and a server dying in the last over did not break the design. The stateless app tier is doing its job.

next.text: Stop routing cache misses to db at read time. Decide where the score lives so a restarted cache can repopulate from a durable, readable source without hammering the database, then rerun the cache restart test.

raw.headline: Over budget mainly because the api tier and the relational db are sized far larger than the traffic they actually see.

items.text: Your design costs {{cost:total.inr}} a month against a budget of {{cost:total.budget}}, so it fails the toss. The spending is concentrated in two places, the api tier at {{cost:api.inr}} and the db at {{cost:db.inr}}. Both are oversized for the work they do.
items.ask: Which components would you shrink first to reach the budget, and by how much?

items.text: The db handles only {{load:db.calls}} a second and sits at {{load:db.rho}} of its capacity, yet it still costs {{cost:db.inr}}. Reads go cdn to lb to api to cache to db, so the database adds {{path:GET_SCORE.hops}} of latency on the read path for very little gain.
items.ask: Do you need the db in the read path at all, or can the cache serve every read?

items.text: The cdn only sees {{load:cdn.calls}} while the api still sees {{load:api.calls}} a second at {{load:api.rho}} of its capacity. So most reads are still reaching the expensive api tier rather than being answered at the edge.
items.ask: Why is the cdn not absorbing the read traffic? Is the path wrong or the cache TTL too short?

items.text: The read path works well on speed: median {{path:GET_SCORE.p50}} and p99 {{path:GET_SCORE.p99}}, with the cache at only {{load:cache.rho}} of capacity. The cache tier has plenty of headroom to take more of the load off the api and the db.
items.ask: Could you route more reads straight to the cache to cut api cost?

next.text: Focus on the two cost centres. Shrink the api tier and take the db out of the read path, letting the cache and cdn serve reads, then check the monthly total against the budget.

items.text: Your design costs ₹3,83,000 a month against a budget of ₹2,60,000, and that is what failed the toss. Every other test went unrun, so the first job is spend, not shape. Shrink until the bill fits, then re-score the rest.
items.ask: Which tier would you shrink first to get under the limit, and what would you give up?

Both paths still reach the db: a read travels cdn, lb, api, cache, db, and an update writes to the db directly. That db line is 35 % of spend and it is the easiest large chunk to cut if the score can be held in the cache.

items.ask: Which component would you shrink first, and how do you decide the right size?
items.text: Your design costs {{cost:total.inr}} a month against a {{cost:total.budget}} budget, so the toss test failed and nothing else could pass. The design is structurally right; the sizing is wrong. Cut the api tier down before changing the architecture.

items.ask: How many app servers does the peak read rate actually need?
items.text: The api servers take {{cost:api.inr}} a month, {{cost:api.share}} of total, yet they handle about {{load:api.calls}} and sit at {{load:api.rho}} of capacity. You are paying for headroom you never use. Size the tier to the read peak plus the update rate, not to the fan count.

items.ask: Why do reads reach the database at all once the cache is in the path?
items.text: The database costs {{cost:db.inr}}, {{cost:db.share}} of total, but it only sees {{load:db.calls}}. Reads still fall through the cache into the db on {{path:GET_SCORE.hops}}. Serve scores from the cache and let the db hold only durable writes, so you can drop to a single small primary.

items.ask: Which hop would you remove to shorten the read path?
items.text: Read p99 is {{path:GET_SCORE.p99}} and update p99 is {{path:UPDATE_SCORE.p99}}. The update path spends most of its time in the db hop, and the read path adds one more. With the score allowed to be {{test:t01-toss.expected}} old at most, this tail needs to come down.

items.ask: What happens to reads when the cache restarts mid over?
items.text: The read median is {{path:GET_SCORE.p50}}, inside the instant requirement, and the cache is barely loaded at {{load:cache.rho}} of capacity. The cache in front of the score is the right shape; keep it and make sure it absorbs the read path completely.

review.headline: Judge could not read the design: neither the read nor the write path reaches any place data is stored.

items.text: Your GET_SCORE route stops before any sql, nosql or objectstore. The judge could not find a place where a score actually lives, so a read has nothing to fetch. Trace your read line and make sure it ends at a store holding the score.
items.ask: Where does the app read the score value from, and which part of your diagram holds it?

items.text: Your UPDATE_SCORE route also never reaches a store, so an update is dropped rather than saved. Since no score update may be lost, the write must land in durable storage, for example nosql or sql, and the cache should be filled from that write.
items.ask: Which component persists the scorer's update, and what happens if it fails?

items.text: The judge reported errors on two lines, so the shape of the whole design could not be checked for latency, freshness or cost. Fix the routes first, then re-examine whether reads are served from cache and whether writes are durable.
items.ask: After fixing the routes, how do you show reads stay fast and the score stays fresh?

next.text: Redraw the two routes so GET_SCORE and UPDATE_SCORE both terminate at a durable store (nosql or sql), with the cache fed by the write. Then resubmit for a real latency and cost check.

review.headline: The judge could not read the design: neither the read path nor the write path reaches any datastore.

items.text: Your GET_SCORE route stops before reaching any place scores actually live. With a store in the path, a read can be served from a cache warmed from that store, which is how a hot key can stay under the read latency target.
items.ask: Where does your GET_SCORE route fetch the score from, and how does it reach the store that holds it?

items.text: UPDATE_SCORE is never saved, so the scorer's write has nowhere to land and no score can be served or aged. The write path needs a durable datastore behind it, and a read path that can see what was written.
items.ask: Which part persists a score update, and how do reads see that value within the staleness window?

next.text: Redraw the two routes so each one ends at a datastore (sql, nosql or objectstore), then layer the cache and queue on top of those paths.

review.headline: Your routes never reach durable storage, so reads have nothing to serve and updates are lost

items.text: GET_SCORE stops at the load balancer and cache, and never reaches sql, nosql or objectstore. So there is no source of truth behind the cache. If the cache restarts mid over, it has nothing to refill from and fans see a miss or a stale empty value.
items.ask: Where does the cache get its value from when it restarts mid over?

items.text: UPDATE_SCORE also never reaches sql, nosql or objectstore. The scorer's ball by ball write goes nowhere durable, which breaks the requirement that no score update may be lost. The write path needs a durable landing point behind the cache.
items.ask: Which durable store does the scorer write to, and is that write synchronous?

items.text: Both routes together mean the judge could not read the design at all, so no requirement was actually exercised. Fix the request paths first: reads and writes must both terminate in a durable store, with the cache in front of the read path only.
items.ask: Can you draw both request paths end to end, from the load balancer to where the data lives?

next.text: Redraw the two flows so each ends in a durable store: the read path serving from cache with a store behind it, and the write path persisting the score. Ignore load and budget for now.
